utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, good morning to you. Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you so much. For the record, accused Nikolic is still indisposed. And we'll be issuing -- giving some instructions -- one moment. We will be giving some instructions to the Registrar to update us on his condition in due course after we finish with this witness. General Gvero also is absent for the time being this morning. And for justified reason, and he will be returning to the courtroom later on. I take it Mr. Krgovic, that he has, I understand that he has given his consent to proceed in his absent; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. General Gvero has a medical exam so he has given his agreement that the trial continues in his absent. My colleague Mr. Josse is also absent. He is monitoring the trial of General Nikolaj [phoen] in another case, so he will not be joining us today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to inform the Trial Chamber that Ms. Julie Condon will be absent until the end of next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Mr. Josse is not here, and the rest are here. The Prosecution is Mr. McCloskey and Mr. Nicholls. No one else behind the column. Good morning to you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are going to continue with the few cross-examinations still remaining. Mr. Haynes, you were about to finish your cross-examination yesterday. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Through, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-150 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yesterday afternoon when we finished we were just looking at the transcript of an intercept you had recorded and it's e-court reference P1353B.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If there is a problem, let's have the -- oh, no, it's okay. All right. Go ahead, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: It's not on my screen yet. I don't know if it's in front of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Wait a minute. Mr. Nicholls, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I was just saying it's tab 7, if everybody has the book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly. I was going to suggest that if we have technical problems then we can use the text. But do you have it now in front of you, Witness? No. I need -- I think he needs your assistance. Madam Usher has certainly got it, I can see it from here. But it's not on mine, I must say. He has it, all right. I think we can safely proceed, Mr. Haynes, because we have the hard copy of it. He's got a copy in front of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'm content. I'm concerned that none of the accused can see it, of course. But if the witness can see it, then I can take the points very quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Usher, could you take the hard copy and put it on the ELMO, please. And the accused can follow from the ELMO, from the -- tab 7, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And it's the second page of that particular intercept, which is numbered 372, the last three numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 372. Madam Registrar, perhaps you can inquire whether this is a technical problem that will continue in which case we need to address it, or whether it is only with this particular document. It's the system, okay. So we need to alert the technicians. Thank you. I draw the attention of the accused that it is now on the ELMO, and you can see it if you are -- yeah, okay. So we can safely proceed. Thank you, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: You will recall we were looking at this intercept yesterday afternoon, Witness. And I want to ask you three or four very simple questions about it. Firstly, was this a conversation in which it was easy to discern what people were saying?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-150 [Resumed]
utterances.text: My task was to record it, but as for the other things that was up to the people at higher levels.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note the witness is speaking too close to the microphone and we cannot really understand well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The interpreters have drawn my attention that, Witness, you are speaking too close to the microphone, and that is creating some problems for them. If you can maintain that position, I think that will be better. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Is this document in your handwriting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-150 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: So it was you that listened to it and wrote out the conversation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-150 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And there don't appear to be any passages where you have had difficulty in discerning what people were saying in this conversation; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-150 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, well there was something, and I did put a question mark there where something was understood, where it was inaudible.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. But that was the only part of the conversation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-150 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand the question, if the question was meant for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: The question really was that there was only one part of the conversation that you had difficulty understanding.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-150 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And was this a conversation that contained important information?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-150 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my view, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I want to see if you agree with me as to what the important information in this conversation was. Was it important that you've discovered from this conversation that Major Jevdjevic was in Zepa?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-150 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I'm concerned, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And also important that Vinko was not in Zepa?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-150 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: But you also discovered from this conversation, didn't you, not only was Vinko not in Zepa, it was not intended that he should go to Zepa?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-150 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot know that, if he intended to go there or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: No, but you listened to the conversation and you can gain an understanding of what people are intending to do from what you hear, can't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-150 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just recorded what I heard. I didn't make anything up.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I'm going to move on now. And if the e-court system is still not working I want you to have a look quickly at the intercept that's behind our tab 8.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The system seems to be working now, at least on our monitor. If you could perhaps check on yours, and the accused likewise.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes, it's working, Your Honour. In that case I want P2931B. And again, if the Witness could have a look at the bottom half of that page and the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Have you read that, Witness, the bottom half of that page?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-150 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't manage to read the whole thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Tell us when you've read that page, and then the usher can show you the next page.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-150 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, very well. We can go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. And again tell us when you've finished reading that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-150 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I only have two questions about this intercept. You will agree, this appears to be a conversation about the provision of some fuel, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-150 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it seems.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: One of the names you've written down in this conversation is the name Trbic. Was that a name that meant anything to you in September of 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-150 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember that now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And lastly this: On the computer printout of this conversation the date that's given to this conversation is the 22nd of September, but we don't see that in the notebook. Is that because the date will have appeared further back in the notebook?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-150 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really couldn't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Meek or Mr. Ostojic, I don't know. Yesterday you were still in consultations with your client with a view to deciding whether to cross-examine this witness or not. Do you have a cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, and we have determined that we have no questions for this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. I think we have covered everyone except Ms. Nikolic or Mr. Bourgon, yeah. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-150 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I only have a few questions for you this morning, further to your testimony, and my first question goes as follows: You mentioned in your statement that in order to be as accurate as possible that you would listen to the tape as often as was necessary. I would just like to confirm with you that indeed this is something that was necessary for every single intercept, that you could never make out what was on it the first time. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-150 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In case something was unclear, we would play that back. If something was clear, then we -- there was no need to play it back a few times. Sometimes some things were inaudible, we couldn't hear it very well, there were was some kind of crackling or buzzing. That's the -- those were the parts that we would play back then to see what was being said.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, I would just like to -- to confirm whether it was more often that you would get -- that you would need to listen to the tape many times, or that you could transcribe the conversation the first time around. Which was more regular?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-150 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was more regular to hear it back several times in order to avoid sending information to our superiors that was inaccurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you mention also in your statement that when a portion of the conversation was inaudible, that this would be indicated on the transcript. And I would like to draw your attention to Exhibit P1200B for Bravo, and I'd like to have this exhibit placed on the e-court, please. Now, from this conversation, Witness, you indicated as participants in this conversation someone called -- sorry for the pronunciation, but Djurdjic, and beside you have a Jelena, and then it says "inaudible." My question to you is what was inaudible here? Is it the Jelena that was inaudible, is it the second name of the Jelena, or is it something to do with the Djurdjic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-150 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that it states here clearly that Jelena was inaudible.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, if Jelena was inaudible, how could you write "Jelena"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-150 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Djurdjic probably addressed her as Jelena and that's how we established that the name was Jelena.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, as a -- when I look at all -- the eight conversations that we have in this document today, and first I'd like you to confirm that you did look at each and every one of these conversations; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry, just in reference to the series of questions on this intercept, I wonder, looking at the questions that have been asked, if the Witness be could be allowed to read the entire intercept. I think's he's probably just seen what I see on my page, which is the first, small portion of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Fair enough. Good point, Mr. Nicholls, if the Witness thinks it is necessary. Witness, would you like to read the entire transcript or intercept?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, let's give him the opportunity to read -- to go through it. Perhaps it's easier if we give him a hard copy of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, my question was not -- did not relate to the intercept at all, other than at the very beginning. But if we want to take the time for him to read it, that's fine with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It depends on what the rest of the questions are, Mr. Bourgon. I mean, I understand what you say, obviously, but I don't know what other questions you have in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Maybe my colleague should wait before he does his objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But it's fair enough. I mean, if he's going to be asked on this intercept, I think he perhaps should be given the opportunity to read it through again. Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just to briefly respond and not waste time, I think the question, "How did you come up with the name Jelena?" calls for him to be allowed to read the whole conversation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's give him a short time. As soon as you are ready, Witness, please tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you can see clearly here, "let me just note down these details. Just wait a little bit, Jelena."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Witness, I did not intend to ask this question, but now that we are into this intercept, I see from the conversation that the word "Jelena" appears a couple of times on the complete intercept. But at the top part it says Jelena as being inaudible. So I just want to -- to explain --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: -- what exactly is inaudible at that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It's actually been answered, that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I see a little bit point in what he is asking. I think it's next -- simple explanation that we need to have from the witness. Yes, Witness, can you answer that question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think this conversation was maybe not recorded from the very beginning. We recorded this part, and that's why we did not hear Jelena at the very beginning until the other speaker mentioned her name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I think it's clear now, Mr. Bourgon, and you can move to something different.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, Witness, the -- what is important to me is not that intercept itself, but it's the fact that if you did write a name in the notebook that is because you heard the name correctly; is that so?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-150 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And if there was a doubt as to the name that you heard, you would put something beside that name to indicate that you were not sure at that particular moment; is that so?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-150 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And my last question is what I asked previously, that you did have an opportunity to look at the eight intercepts that are in the package that I have with me this morning; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, one moment. General Miletic would like to address the Trial Chamber. THE ACCUSED MILETIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have a problem with interpretation. I hear you and the Prosecutor and the witness, but I cannot hear Mr. Bourgon. I can hear him as long as I keep the button pressed but then I don't hear you and I can't really follow the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. That is -- that is strange. Let's try -- try it out. Mr. Bourgon, can I ask you to say something.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the interpreters to translate in B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Just in relation to my last question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You can repeat the question, for example and we see whether General Miletic is receiving --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: It doesn't appear to be working, Mr. President, but the ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Popovic, Mr. Beara, are you receiving, you have no problems? And General Pandurevic? Okay. Borovcanin? Okay. General Miletic, can you -- can you -- are you receiving interpretation of what I am saying now? THE ACCUSED MILETIC: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And Mr. Bourgon, can I kindly ask you again to say something.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Concerning my last question, the question was ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I thank you, General Miletic, for having drawn our attention to that. Please sit down. And Mr. Bourgon can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Witness, I will say my question once again and simply that the -- I have here a series of intercepts that you have identified other than one of them, and I would simply confirm that you did look at all of these intercepts and confirmed that they were yours and you have looked at them; is that so?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-150 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. I have no more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Just trying to refresh my memory, I don't think there were any other cross-examinations. Mr. Nicholls, would you like to re-examine your witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Witness, that means that your testimony finishes here, ends here. Madam Usher will escort you out of the courtroom and you will receive the assistance. I am still -- you will be escorted out of the courtroom and we will assist you to facilitate your return back home at the earliest. On behalf of the Tribunal, I wish to thank you for coming to give your testimony and also wish you a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's proceed with the document-tendering process. The first two documents as per the list that has been circulated by the Prosecution, namely the witness statement of the 23rd of January of this year, and the pseudonym sheet, are being admitted under seal. As PO2389 and PO2390 respectfully. The rest are intercepts, they are listed as I explained.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Together with a handwritten intercept notebook. What appears in bold characters will be kept under seal. I take it that there are no objections from any of the Defence teams? I hear none. So these will all be marked for identification -- identification. Thank you. Any of the Defence teams wishes to tender any documents? None. So that closes this chapter. Now, let's start from here. This is an order that we are issuing verbally, or instructions that we are -- I don't like using the word "order" that much; instructions that we are going to give to the Registrar of this Tribunal. His attention is drawn by the Trial Chamber to the fact that Accused Nikolic has been absent from the courtroom for part of the last week and also this week due to a medical problem that he seems to be encountering. The Trial Chamber wishes the -- the Registrar to make full inquiries with the authorities of the Detention Unit, including the medical doctor attached to that unit and report back to the Trial Chamber at the earliest possible on the state of health of Accused Nikolic, providing details of the medical attention that he has been receiving at the unit or even outside the detention unit. And an estimate or a prognosis of when Mr. Nikolic is likely to be able to return to attend -- be present for -- for these proceedings. Thank you. I don't think there is need to do the same in relation to General Gvero, Mr. Krgovic. I don't think so. If there is a problem -- the reason is first we need to know if this is on -- a long-haul problem or whether it is transient, in which case we'll proceed as we have been doing. If it's on the long haul we will need to discuss further. Now, yesterday I drew your attention to a Prosecution motion -- Prosecution motion to add another intercept operator, namely Witness 177 as a 92 ter witness. We heard submissions. I take it, Mr. Nicholls, that this witness is here, ready to give evidence? We're talking of Witness number 177.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: The witness is -- is here, Your Honour. Not ready immediately to give evidence. We do have another intercept operator who could give evidence I believe at about 11.00. But he -- he is here. The witness you're referring to, and possibly later today, but he arrived last night.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He was scheduled to start giving evidence tomorrow, Thursday. But obviously you need, both of you -- both sides need to know what the position is. Are there any further submissions you would like to make in relation to this Witness number 77 [sic]? I hear none. I think we can hand down our decision orally, and we'll follow it up with a written version. Our decision is the following: We consider that it is in the interests of justice for the proposed witness to be added to the 65 ter witness list, and that good cause has been shown by the Prosecution for the addition of the said witness to the 65 ter witness list in light of paragraph 105 of the decision on Trial Chamber's decision on Prosecution's confidential motion for the admission of written evidence in lieu of viva voce testimony pursuant to Rule 92 bis, which we handed down on the 12th of September. We hold that the Prosecution has identified a reasonable basis for admitting the testimony of the proposed witness pursuant to Rule 92 ter, but that the identification of the specific written evidence of the proposed witness to be admitted is a pre-condition for its admission pursuant to the said rule. We invoke Rule 75 (A). We feel that there is -- we are satisfied that there is an objective basis in the circumstances and past employment of the proposed witness demonstrating that he may be at risk of harassment and intimidation and that the protective measures sought are consistent with the rights of the accused. Consequently pursuant to Articles 21, 21 (2) and 22 of the Statute and Rules 54 and 75, we hereby grant the Prosecution motion. And the details will be incorporated in the written decision; however, we are saying that the Prosecution witness will testify with the protective measures of face distortion and shall be referred to by pseudonym at all times in the course of his testimony, or whenever referred to in the course of the proceedings, whether during the hearing or in documents, including the transcripts of proceedings. In other words, I take it that you have not asked for voice distortion in this particular case.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I don't believe so, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. The rest, you can -- you will be able to follow in the -- in the written version of the proceedings. One moment, I need to consult with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls, or Mr. McCloskey, is the next witness, Mr. Nicholls said at 11.00. I don't know. Is he the -- another intercept witness or is he the one -- the crime-base witness that you referred to yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We have a witness that's outside and who is available that is the crime-base witness, which is the subject --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So that brings me to the latest development in this case. I hope that you are all privy to the Borovcanin Defence team submission concerning issues in relation to the testimony of Prosecution Witness PW-111, which was handed -- which was filed yesterday but which was made available to us this morning, sometime before we started the sitting. I don't know if Mr. Lazarevic would like to address the Trial Chamber on -- on his motion. If not, and I think the motion in itself is --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Just very briefly, very briefly. The main reason why we submitted the submission was to avoid any delays caused by oral submitting issues. But there are two things that I believe should be clarified by the Prosecution which may assist the Trial Chamber in issuing the right decision. During yesterday's session Mr. McCloskey informed us on two things. First of all, that this witness testified before Bosnian court. I would really like to know if Mr. McCloskey can tell us what the date it was when he testified, which would help us to establish what was the time period from his testimony there and we would -- it would enable us to know whether they were diligent enough to bring this testimony here. Other issue is the request that was made by the Prosecution to the Bosnian government, when it was submitted. If they have problems with corporation with Bosnian government, it was submitted but with no response, that -- I believe we are entitled to know that. And I believe that have quite a lot of -- well, possibilities to deal with situation when the government does not cooperate with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Lazarevic. Mr. McCloskey, would you like to respond to that? And also to the motion that was filed by -- by Mr. Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: My best information on when he testified comes from Mr. Stojanovic, who is from Bosnia and is following those proceedings in the language that they are in. And I -- we've all known that this was something that was happening and they had every ability to make a request as do we, in the language that they use. I believe Mr. Stojanovic thinks that it was October that he -- that he testified. And -- but it's -- as yet I'm not exactly sure. We can find that out. And I'm not exactly sure when we put our -- our request for assistance in either. But it was a while back. And I -- I really -- I don't look at this in any -- and neither has Defence counsel, as anyone's fault, really. This is -- and we've spoken about this, and in fact we've spoken to all Defence counsel and everyone is communicating well and is trying to deal with all of these issues with positive suggestions and we've had a number of them. And so I understand their motion, I understand the concern. I spoke to the witness about it. And the witness is -- the witness says he will -- he'll come back in a few weeks and that he's ready to do that. Now, the problem with that is, of course, is that that leaves us with a huge gap. And courtrooms have gaps, in normal courtrooms that's -- I know that's a terrible sin here, and I -- and I work constantly to avoid it, but he's here, he's ready. I would prefer that -- that he go through all of his testimony and cross-examination and that he come back for any cross necessary because of his transcript. On the other hand, we're okay, and he's okay with coming back in a few weeks when we can sort out this transcript. We're trying to put on a perfect trial; we can't. We're trying. But we'll continue to try. And we appreciate the Defence, we appreciate the tone of the motion and we appreciate that we are all still trying -- after all these months there's no finger pointing going on, we're trying to do this. And that's very much appreciated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. McCloskey. Yes, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I would just like the Chamber to note that Mr. Borovcanin's counsel are not alone and that the Defence for Mr. Beara wholeheartedly supports the motion and joins in this motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think the Trial Chamber looks at the Borovcanin motion as one which is across the board and applies or would apply to -- to all the accused because it is a matter of principles of justice first and foremost. I don't read the Borovcanin motion as a criticism of the Prosecution, and I do not look at the whole event as -- as -- as a shortcoming on the part of the Prosecution. All that has happened is understandable. And if it's a sin, you have got confessors here that are prepared to be understanding. There are two issues, basically. One is whether to even start with the testimony of this witness in chief. The other is, if we start with the testimony of this witness in chief, whether we should reserve cross-examination completely for all Defence teams and not just for the Borovcanin team. That's the understanding. I mean, there is no sense in approaching it in any different manner. We have of course discussed amongst ourselves, in the short time available that we had prior to entering this courtroom, and ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The position we have taken, briefly put, is as follows: We see, and we -- we see a lot of validity in the argument brought forward by the Borovcanin Defence team in their motion for the suspension of any cross-examination at -- at this stage, pending the disclosure of the material that they referred to in their motion. It is, however, our opinion that at this stage the same arguments need not necessarily prevent the commencement of the testimony of this witness in -- in chief. We are not at the moment giving or handing down an order to this effect, we are just inviting the two sides to have a short tete-a-tete consultation between you in the spirit of cooperation that has characterised this trial from the very beginning, thanks to the attitude that you have adopted. And the idea being to proceed with the examination-in-chief, with the direct, as Mr. McCloskey would call it, and the understanding is that when that is over the witness will be sent home and he will then be called again for cross-examination at a later stage, if there is a request for cross-examination which I understand -- I would almost take it for granted there will be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So what we suggest is we'll suspend the sitting for a few minutes, unless -- unless there is the go-ahead from -- from the Defence teams, because if we can deal with this here and now without suspending the sitting, then we will proceed that way. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, it's -- I hope not to take more than a couple of hours with this -- with this witness, and I think he would prefer to get this done in a -- in a solid block, and I -- I know that that presents problems and -- and he will do of course whatever you say. But I just want -- he -- he was cross-examined by 11 Defence counsel in Sarajevo and is ready to go, but given his experience he would like to do it in one block, but he is ready to do it ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's a choice or a decision that you would have -- you would have to take. We have not handed down a decision, as we have said, but I think we have depicted a scenario that is clear enough, there won't be -- it's very unlikely that there will be cross-examination today anyway. So that's the position. If you prefer not to bring forward or proceed with your direct today, I mean, it will be your decision, and -- and we will give our position on that. But we are not interfering for the time being with -- if on the other hand the Defence teams agree that he should proceed with the direct today, then we don't need a -- an interval of time, a pause for consultations. Yeah, Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe that we would have to consult among ourselves. It is not something the Borovcanin decision has to decide by himself. If we could have 10 minutes and we will then be able to approach the Prosecution and discuss this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Fair enough. We will have a short pause, a short break. We will be outside the courtroom. Once you have reached an agreement after these consultations, could you kindly alert Madam Registrar and we will resume. Thank you. --- Break taken at 10.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, for the record, General Gvero is back in the courtroom. Yes. Do you have any information for the Trial Chamber? Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It appears that the Defence would prefer the one block approach as well, though I think everyone is ready to hear from him if that need be, but if preferences were given, I'm told that they would prefer the one-block approach as well. But there is also a problem with next week that we need to discuss, but one problem at a time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Oh, dear, dear, dear, dear, dear, dear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. You've shown a lot of cooperation and the Trial Chamber will do the same. We fully understand your position, your respective positions, and we are inclined to comply with your expressed wishes. So we will not proceed with the testimony of this witness. That's number one. Number two, I take it then that the Borovcanin motion is moot, and need not be decided. Agreed, Mr. Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. Number three is, when can we have the pleasure of seeing another witness walking into the courtroom?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer has asked for 11.30. I told him 11.00, and he's asked for 11.30. So I think we ought to give him until 11.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think we have an option. All right. We will resume the sitting at 11.30. And this will be the intercept operator that was the subject matter of the motion that we decided orally this morning, no? 177, Witness 177.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We have two that are ready today, and this first one I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Whoever it is. Whoever it is, we will reconvene at 11.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could I alert you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, in the meantime, before -- before we have this break, you intimated, you hinted that there may be again problems next week. What are you really referring to, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, as -- as you know, when we saw the acceleration, we accelerated our -- our movement to bring witnesses here, but we are also planning next week for four significant acts or conducts witnesses. The Nikolic issue. I see this morning that he is -- he is still not here. Due to visa issues and requirements, I have to cancel all those people now. In fact, I told them last night that it wasn't looking good, and so those folks have now been cancelled. Now, we anticipated that high probability, just in speaking with Ms. Nikolic, but now that's off. And that would have taken a week, I think, given anyone's estimates. But we have been trying and -- to push people into next week, naturally, to help -- and so we had the double Nikolic problem and the acceleration problem. This is a normal problem for a Prosecutor, and it's something that you know you do. And so we have given our notice to the Defence of our -- of the people that we hope and we think are going to be here. Some we've got confirmations from, some we have not. One was another Kravica warehouse survivor, who I believe has the same problem. And a couple of the other ones, the Defence has said already, "oh, my," and they may want to have some -- something to say about that, because this is an acceleration on them as well. So while we do have some available and we will continue to work, that has -- this -- again, this unforeseeable problem has -- has put us behind the eight ball a bit and I would turn that over to the Defence to give you their view-points on it. Again, as we are working together and communicating very well on all these things and it's just where we find ourselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you, Mr. McCloskey. Is there any -- any of the Defence counsel wishes to address the Chamber? Yes, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President and Your Honours. I -- just briefly, so the Court can see, it's not a question of shifting blame or responsibility. These are unpredictable circumstances that occurred. But for the Defence of Beara and possibly others, to have the Prosecutor in our view, although not intentionally, violate the spirit and the letter of this Court's ruling, meaning that of this you should give us notice at least at the beginning of the month for next month's witnesses, we are now being given less than a week for some relevantly critical witnesses that -- we have obviously reviewed, consulted with our client, but we think it's going to be become, because of the accelerated process, the rule and not the exception to the rule. Now, if it happens, we want to strongly object to that. We think we should be given adequate notice. At the very least we should be given a week to 10 days' notice of witnesses that are forthcoming, not four or five days as is in this case. And then, again, it's not my learned colleague's fault intentionally, and he is scrambling to bring those witnesses. We do object to proceeding next week with those witnesses that he has identified, specifically with Witness number 113. I'm not sure if he has a pseudonym assigned to him, but we will figure that out. But we've worked out some formalities with the Prosecutor in our attempt to talk to victim and witness on this specific witness. We are hoping to resolve it but I object because it is on enormously short notice to bring this witness when we anticipated him coming in March or possibly April and now he's coming next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any further submissions? All right. I trust that you will continue these mutual consultations between you, and try to present the Trial Chamber with a programme, a schedule which is a feasible one and which is acceptable to -- to all. I mean try to do your best, please, and then we'll take it up from there. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If I could just -- on another issue, as you know, Ms. Fauveau is by herself. She's been trying to have Mr. Petrusic be co-counsel and I don't want to speak for her, but she's pretty healthy, but if she gets sick, we're in trouble on the current situation. So we need, and I know she's trying, but we need a co-counsel that can step in for her. I'm just trying to anticipate other issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, but that is being taken care of, Mr. McCloskey. We should be in a position to determine it, I suppose, in the course of next week. Yes, Mr. Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, since the Prosecutor started talking about this problem, it could be a problem indeed, but I think that I have a choice to choose a co-counsel and if I cannot have Mr. Petrusic, I prefer to be alone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Madam Fauveau. In the meantime, try to remain healthy, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we support her choice of Mr. Petrusic. I know registry is having some issues with that, but we know Mr. Petrusic and we fully support him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. That's helpful, Mr. McCloskey. As I said, we will have a break now, resuming at 11.30. Or earlier, if Mr. Thayer is in the position to proceed before 11.30, in which case please alert everyone. Yes, Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: If I can just have one clarification for the record. In his submission, Mr. McCloskey, while he did inform the Chamber that he received information from Mr. Stojanovic, my co-counsel, regarding the witness that was supposed to testify today, that's true, but I would like to avoid any misunderstanding. We received information that one of Kravica survivor witnesses testified in Sarajevo through newspapers. And having in mind there are just two of them, we just told two days ago to Mr. McCloskey that we have this information, but we are not 100 per cent sure whether it is this witness or the one who was supposed to come next week. Just to have this for the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Mr. Lazarevic. So we will reconvene at 11.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I just wanted to introduce you to a new member of our staff, a young lawyer, Rupert Elderkin. And he -- he speaks a form of English, I've asked him to go slow. I think it's the real English tongue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you. Are there any submissions on the quality of arms issues? Yes, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Is there a separate channel we could listen to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I take it that this is Witness 172; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. And he will have a pseudonym PW-147. Good morning to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And welcome to this Tribunal. You are very soon going to start giving evidence. Our rules require that before you do so you enter a solemn declaration to the effect that you will be testifying the truth. Madam Usher is going to hand you the text of this solemn declaration. Please read it out aloud and that will be your undertaking with this Tribunal that you will testify the truth. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, sir. Please make yourself comfortable, just take a seat. I just wanted to confirm to you what you probably already know, namely that we have put in place for you three protective measures. One is the use of a pseudonym, in fact you will be referred to as PW-147, and the other two protective measures are facial and voice distortion. I take it these have been already explained to you. I just want a confirmation from you that this arrangement is to your satisfaction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Prosecution will go first, and they will then be followed by cross-examination from Defence teams. Since your voice carries quite a bit, I am making a recommendation to you, don't start giving your answers or answering questions until you see the red light on the microphone of whoever is putting questions to you switched off. Don't speak while the red light is still on. Do you understand me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which microphone?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of whoever is putting questions to you. For example, Mr. Nicholls has just switched on a microphone. You see a red light there. Don't start --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- answering the questions before that red light is switched off. Okay. Thank you. Go ahead. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Witness answered through interpreter].

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. Could I ask the usher to show the witness a document marked for identification as P2394, please. Witness, could you please look at that piece of paper and without reading what is written on it, could you please confirm what is on that piece of paper?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-147
utterances.text: Yes, on the paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: That will go under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Witness, I must start by asking if you recall providing information to the Office of the Prosecutor on May the 7th and 11th of 1999?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-147
utterances.text: Yes, I remember giving it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And was the statement you gave at that time truthful?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-147
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Have you had an opportunity to read your statement before testifying here today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-147
utterances.text: I read it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And did you read this statement in your own language?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-147
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And are you satisfied that the statement that you read was correct and accurate and that information in the statement is true and correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-147
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And if you were asked the same questions, would your answers be the same today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-147
utterances.text: Yes, I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Thank you. And I will now proceed to read a short summary of the statement. The witness was born in 1959.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go in to private session for a short while.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: He described the northern location as shift structure and personnel, their equipment and the practice he followed for intercepting, recording, and transcribing radio communications. He confirmed that he was working in July 1995, but could not recall any particular conversations. At the time he was able to identify individual voices, including Zivanovic, Krstic, Pantic, and Legenda. He reviewed intercept notebook number 97 and identified an intercept at 0615 between Krstic and Trbic and then Krstic and Pandurevic as being handwritten by him. He had no recollection of the particular text. By reviewing the notebook he confirmed that the conversation was recorded on 17th of July, 1995. That ends the summary of his statement, which is P02393.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: I now have a few questions for you, Witness. Did you review seven handwritten copies of intercepts in a tabbed blue binder in my office today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-147
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And did you identify all seven of those as your original handwriting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-147
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Did you also review those same intercepts in the original notebooks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-147
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And did you confirm they were your own in the original notebooks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-147
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Can you confirm, as you sit before the Trial Chamber today, that you have listened to, recorded and transcribed those seven intercepts?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-147
utterances.text: How do you mean? In what way should I confirm, just by checking the handwriting or in some other way?

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: If you can confirm that the handwriting in those notebooks was yours.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-147
utterances.text: The handwriting is mine in all the notebooks that I looked at.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And are you able to say whether you wrote those intercepts in the notebook on the dates confirmed in that notebook?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-147
utterances.text: Yes. On the dates and at the time that I intercepted them, transcribed them and wrote them down.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Thank you. And were you also shown corresponding typed printouts of those seven intercepts today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-147
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Cross-examination. Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Witness. In your statement, which has just been shown to you, you said, among other things, what the type of equipment was that you used at the location where you worked. I would just like to note that the antenna descriptions are missing here, the antennas that were used. So I would like to ask you to tell us if you still remember which antennas were used besides the equipment that you have already mentioned you had?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-147
utterances.text: The antennas that we used in the beginning were mostly television antennas, which had special amplifiers and routers built in. And then later so-called parabolic antennas, parabolas were set up.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And can you as specific as possible, if you can, about the time when these parabolic antennas were set up?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-147
utterances.text: The parabolas were set up in late 1994 or early 1995. I don't remember specifically, but I know it was winter when they were set up.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It was one antenna of that type?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-147
utterances.text: Yes. But it was of a large diameter.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you be able to tell us approximately what that was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-147
utterances.text: I think that the diameter of the antenna was more than two metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was this an antenna that was handmade or was this an authentic product of some factory?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-147
utterances.text: The dish itself was original. It was taken down from some building, and the receivers were made by electronics people, but the dish itself was an authentic, original dish.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said in your statement, and I'm going to quote that part of your statement in order to remind you of it. I don't want to be re-telling it. It says, "The question was asked to me if ever the same message was recorded and transcribed twice. I can confirm that this happened sometimes, usually when the same conversations were being monitored on different frequencies and from different locations." Do you remember that part of your statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-147
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would now like to ask you to explain, when you say "monitored on different frequencies," can you clarify a little bit exactly what this means?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-147
utterances.text: Depending on the location of the unit, all the frequencies were not possible to monitor from the same location, because of the configuration of the terrain. So units that were in other locations, it was then -- for them easier to monitor these other frequencies because they were on a different location.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So if I understood you correctly, the same conversation could be intercepted from different locations but on the same frequency, so when you say different locations, can you please tell me what you mean? Do you mean a location where you were not? For example the southern location, which also existed and which also did the same work as your one. So is that what you mean, or do you mean the same location, but a different room or something?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-147
utterances.text: No, no. A different location. We were in one place, but this was a completely different location, a different elevation, where different people were situated.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So it means a different place which would be quite far from your location. We're not using the exact names here of the locations. You saw that because of the protective measures. So it would be a different place, different town, different mountain, this is what I'm thinking.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-147
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Different town, different mountain.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And just one more question. You also said in your statement the name of the person who mostly entered the handwritten information into the computer, and passed them on to your command. You probably remember the name of the person, but please don't say the name now. If necessary I can refresh your memory but in that case we would need to move into private session. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-147
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember that. And I think that name is in the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Zivanovic. Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: [French on English channel]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment because we are receiving interpretation in French now. Can you repeat, Mr. Meek, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We have no questions for this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. I had heard you but I wanted it to go into the record. Madam Nikolic or Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. We have no questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam Nikolic. Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: This witness does not call for cross-examination on our side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lazarevic. Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is it possible, sir, that you may have taped two conversations within a gap of five minutes in two different notebooks? Is that possible? I would like to ask you whether it's possible for you to have written in two different notebooks.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-147
utterances.text: That happened, too, depending on the assessment about the importance of the intercepted information. If we thought that the information was urgent, and it -- then it would be written to one notebook and then it would be passed on to the communications, so it could be then passed on to the command. We would then take a different notebook and jot down the following or subsequent information.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown 1167B. In English -- 1167A for the English version. Sir, can you see the intercept which has been taped at 2236? This is an intercept which is at the bottom of the page. Is it one of the intercepts which you transcribed, which you wrote down?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-147
utterances.text: I have 2236 here. You said 2246, I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: No, it is 2236, that's what I asked you about.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-147
utterances.text: Yes, yes, it's my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it true that for the person who apparently took part in this conversation first you wrote the name Malic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-147
utterances.text: Because of frequent interruptions or interference on the connection, sometimes when we were taking down the intercepts we were not immediately sure about the name. So then we would go back a couple of times to that place to see what the name was, and sometimes the colleagues helped us to establish the name of the person that was participating in the conversation and that's why the name was corrected here.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Thank you for this explanation. Coming back to this intercept, first of all you wrote "Malic" and after that "Malovic," and that was corrected finally in "Malinic." Isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-147
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Now, about this specific intercept, and I'm asking you this today, did you conclude by yourself that it was Malic or with the help of colleagues?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-147
utterances.text: After so much time I really cannot confirm definitely that I did it myself. I mean, you see yourself how much time has passed, but I have told you what happened in specific situations, how we tried to get the names as accurately as possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: This intercept, this one in particular, you didn't know that it was urgent. True?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-147
utterances.text: Sometimes it would happen that we who worked on this would think something to be quite urgent, but then in frequent cases those working in the communications would also decide whether something was urgent or not, and then would see if it needed to be dispatched right away or if it could be processed according to regular procedure.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: But when you were evaluating whether an intercept was urgent or not, you did write that it was urgent on the notebook, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-147
utterances.text: We would rarely mark an intercept as urgent. If we felt it was urgent, we would immediately take it to the communications person to be printed and forwarded on.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown Exhibit 1168B, and for the English 1168A. About this specific intercept which was taped at 2241, 22 hours 41, is it true that you taped and transcribed this intercept yourself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-147
utterances.text: It's mine. The handwriting is mine.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it true that there was a mistake again in the Malinic name which had first been transcribed as Malovic? So there was a mistake. Is it true that you transcribed first -- you wrote first Malovic and then you corrected it in Malinic. Didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-147
utterances.text: Yes. The first word was Malovic, then it was crossed out and corrected into Malinic.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you remember whether this intercept was taped on the same day as the preceding intercept, which we have just seen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-147
utterances.text: I cannot remember exactly, there is no date here. But I see that it is my handwriting. I can confirm that these are my manuscripts. Whether it is the same day or not, I can't be sure. There are no facts that would enable me to say that it was done the same day.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: If one assumes that these two conversations took place on the same day with only five minutes between each other, is it possible that indeed you didn't hear properly the name in one of these intercepts and therefore you concluded it was Malinic because the name was similar to the name you had heard in the former conversation or intercept?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-147
utterances.text: I just told you a moment ago. Not only me, but all the other people who were working on this job, if we were not sure about a name, if we couldn't make it out, then we would put our heads together to try to make out the name. And we would rewind and play it back and again and again to try to make out the name until we are sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it true that this specific intercept was difficult to transcribe?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-147
utterances.text: It's most likely that the only difficulty we had was in identifying that name. We did not hear the name of the other participant, and that's why he was designated as X. So the only problem was with the full names of the participants.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Isn't it true that certain passages of this intercept have been crossed out and just above this passage you have noted the word "perturb," "perturbations" or "jamming"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-147
utterances.text: Specifically above this last part, why it was crossed out, I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: But you can see that at least in two places -- at least four places you used a word between brackets "perturbations" or "jamming," "scrambling"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-147
utterances.text: Yes, because it occurred sometimes that we did not hear one of the speakers due to interference, and it happens even today in telephone traffic, sometimes you have interference on telephone lines, let alone at that time when the equipment was of much lower quality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Elderkin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. I would ask if perhaps it would help if the witness could be shown the whole intercept. I think he's only seeing the first page at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't quite know that it will really help, but if the witness himself is in agreement and Madam Fauveau is too, we may proceed along those lines. Madam Fauveau, do you have much further questions on this intercept?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [No interpretation] THE FRENCH INTERPRETER: We didn't hear Mrs. Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I heard Madam Fauveau, she said she's got about two or three more questions of a general nature and we can proceed along these lines. Witness, look at me, please. If, in trying to answer Madam Fauveau's next questions you need time to go through the entire intercept, read it all, then please you only have to ask and we will grant you time to go through it before you answer the question. But I don't think it will be necessary. But if it is necessary, we'll -- we'll do that. Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: For this one where you had that jamming and you had these problems to hear properly, is it true that you jotted down to the best of your ability what you heard?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-147
utterances.text: In all intercepts we sought to be as sure, and to have intercepts as authentic as possible, to record precisely what we were able to hear well, and if there was any interference and we couldn't be sure, we would record it in such a way as to make it obvious that we were not sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And when you jotted down these intercepts, which would be sometimes very difficult to hear, would you admit that in certain cases you thought you heard something and that maybe indeed you didn't hear properly and that, in fact, the two speakers were talking about something else or saying something else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-147
utterances.text: In response to your previous question, I told you that we tried to record and transcribe the things we heard well as authentically as we could. But we could not make the judgement whether the speakers really meant what they were saying or they were thinking something completely different. That judgement was impossible for us to make. Because it did occur in some conversations that certain speakers would say something but in reality something entirely different happened. The reality was completely different. And I know from speaking with colleagues from other locations that something that happened a couple of days after an intercept displayed a completely different reality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we have covered this subject enough, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President, I agree. And I would like the witness to be shown P1237B, if it could be shown to the witness, please. And for the English it is 1237A.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, in this intercept you identified one of the speakers as being -- THE FRENCH INTERPRETER: We didn't hear the name properly.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Could you tell us how you determined the name? In this conversation you identified Trivic as being one of the speakers. Can you tell us how you identified this person as being Trivic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-147
utterances.text: At the moment when this was done, some speakers that were involved in a great number of conversations became familiar by their speech mannerisms, accents, et cetera. So we would know their names when they made telephone calls, even if they did not identify themselves. Some of them had a very particular accent or dialect, and they were easily identifiable.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, we heard a while ago a person who could be recognised by voice which you could recognise by its voice. When you made a statement in 1999 to the Office of the Prosecutor, you did not mention Trbic [as interpreted]. Trivic.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-147
utterances.text: Maybe it is not written there, but I cannot tell you, after all these years, how exactly I came up with that name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Fauveau, your 20 minutes are up. How much longer?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have still two or three questions. And I think the other teams then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead. But please try to bring your cross-examination to an end as early as possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Wasn't it usual that you would jot down with a question mark, put a question mark when you recognised the person by his or her voice?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-147
utterances.text: Such things occurred, but in most cases whenever we were unable to hear a person well or we were not sure about their identity, we designated them as X.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Perhaps my question was not sufficiently clear. When you recognised a person by his or her voice, wasn't it usual to put a question mark just by the name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-147
utterances.text: We rarely used that, we rarely put a question mark next to a name.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you agree that recognising a voice is not an absolutely sure means, and certain mistakes a possible, some mistakes are possible?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think he needs to answer that question. Take it for granted, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, sir, Mr. President. I still have two questions to ask.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, in this specific intercept, the name of Miletic is mentioned; isn't it so? More or less at the middle of the page.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-147
utterances.text: Yes, it is mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: There is only the name Miletic, you don't have the rank there, indeed? Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-147
utterances.text: I agree, that's what is written, only the last name.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, I would like you to see notebook number 9, P2308, Exhibit P2308. Page ERN 0077-9661. In the e-court system it's page 44. This is an intercept which I think was not transcribed by you, I don't think it was you who transcribed it. Is it so?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-147
utterances.text: You see at the bottom the name of the person who did this job.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Yes, agreed. But could you read the names of the speakers in this intercept?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-147
utterances.text: Sergeant Miletic, Lieutenant-Colonel Janjic, question mark, X, and as far as I can see, Benak is the last participant.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no other question to ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Fauveau. Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have no questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Haynes, I take it you --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you, nor do I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So Mr. Elderkin, do you wish to re-examine your witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: No, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Witness, we have no further questions for you, which means that your testimony finishes -- ends here. Madam Usher will escort you and our staff will assist you to facilitate your return home at the earliest. On behalf of the Tribunal I wish to thank you for having come over to give evidence, and I also wish you a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So the list of documents that the Prosecution wishes to tender with this witness has been circulated. I'll start with the first two, which are standard, and the first one being PO2393, and that's the witness statement dated 11th May, 1999, which is being admitted and kept under seal. Next is PO2394, which is the pseudonym sheet. That is also being admitted and will remain under seal. Any objections in relation to the rest of the documents? I hear none. So the rest of the documents consisting in seven intercepts and various language versions, together with intercept notebooks 1979 and 232 are being marked for identification with the understanding that the ones that appear in bold characters in the list that has been circulated will be preserved under seal. Thank you. Now, do you have the next witness ready to start?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: We do not at the moment, Your Honour. The -- this witness has been seen this morning. The statement, I believe, it must be a very brief statement in English, should be done by now. The B/C/S may or may not be translated. I think Mr. Thayer can pass out the statement if it hasn't been e-mailed right away in English, and the B/C/S would soon follow. And then if there are no surprises in it, which I don't anticipate, we could be ready to go at 1.00, I believe, and possibly finish that witness today. I'm sorry that we have to break again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. But that taken, assuming that we can start at 1.00, if there are no problems, okay, with that caveat. What's going to happen tomorrow and the day after? Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No perspiration on -- I'm using perspiration rather than sweat, because I have been told that horses sweat, humans perspire.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, I've heard that. We -- I think we have an agreement Ms. Frease on again to talk about how she obtained or how we obtained the hard copies of the intercepts and the electronic copies of the intercepts and she can also go over what we've referred to as her authentication binder where she had a collection of intercepts and -- and then had various ways of corroborating them. This is an exhibit that goes way back to Krstic, so it's something that the Defence has had for a long time. And -- and we can do it under the same agreement before, unless the Defence is -- and not -- not do any cross-examination of her. Otherwise, you've heard the -- the predicament we're in, and based on the various reasons, we don't have anybody immediately at hand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you. Are there any submissions on this in relation to Ms. Frease's possible testimony? Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President. It's not with regard to Mrs. Frease. I have nothing against her testimony. It was about the witness who is supposed to come back at 1.00. I talked to the Prosecutor many times yesterday who assured me that the witness would not be here today but tomorrow. I would like you to postpone the cross-examination for this witness for tomorrow because I am not ready since I thought he was going to be here tomorrow and not today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is that correct, Mr. McCloskey? It's you or Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, we were thinking we were going to have our big, long witness, but since nothing was sure, I'm sure we couched in our plan that this person would go on when scheduled, which we all know was Thursday. I think this is just a function of the knock on of the decision that was made this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are we -- are you in a position, particularly Madam Fauveau -- I don't know, because if the statement has not been circulated as yet, it may be a useless question that I am putting, but are you in a position to know of how relevant this witness is for your client? Yes, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. It is a person who apparently intercepted a conversation to which my client took part, and another one in which my client is only mentioned. I just would like it add that I spoke to Mr. Thayer yesterday, I believe that Mr. Nicholls was also present at the time. I asked if -- I asked him if there would be a change to let me know by e-mail so that I can be ready but it was not done. I even got a message telling me that the witness would be here tomorrow, so I was not able to know and to prepare adequately for this witness today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let me consult with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think the decision, Madam Fauveau, is that we proceed at 1.00, if we can, but your cross-examination will be put off until tomorrow. Maybe if it is the case. You may review your position after having heard the witness. So that means we will reconvene at 1.00; is that correct? Mr. Meek, you don't have a copy --

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: That sounds correct to me, Judge, but I have a point of clarification, if I might.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I believe I understood your ruling about the cross-examination and direct examination of intercept witnesses, that the Defence had -- the Prosecution had 30 minutes and we had 20 minutes each or a total of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Two hours, 40 minutes, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
