utterances.text: Two hours, 40 minutes -- 20 minutes. So my question is, for example -- or we had 20 minutes or we could split it up how we wanted to. Now, in the last witness, for example, one, two, three, four, that's 80 minutes were not take up yet Ms. Fauveau should have had the 80 minutes, maybe I'm wrong, I just want clarification on it -- how we should do this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You can -- you can explain it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: Mr. Meek, I think our decision was very clear that that is the appropriate distribution, but if Defence counsel were going to have another arrangement, other than 20 minutes a piece, they are to tell us that in advance of starting the cross-examination. So it's not the case that you can simply go along and if time hasn't been taken, someone changes their predicted time. We did request that in advance we be notified if there was going to be a different arrangement of distribution between various Defence counsel. That was the nature of our decision and that is why we are enforcing the 20 minutes for each Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. Judge, would it be correct then that, for example, on the next witness should I deem it not appropriate to use my 20 minutes, I should direct that to the Trial Chamber immediately and say I want to give it to Ms. Fauveau, for example?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, I --

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: That's my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think it can be done on a bilateral basis between you and Madam Fauveau, for example. Because there are other counsel who may require even more time. For example, when we stopped -- or rather we drew the attention of Madam Fauveau that her 20 minutes had lapsed, there were two other Defence teams who had still not cross-examined the witness. Little did we know or had reason to know at the time that they were not going to cross-examine, especially Mr. Haynes in relation to one of -- because obviously we couldn't -- we couldn't tell whether he was going to cross-examine the witness and how much time it would be require. What we ask you to do is the following: If you want to distribute the available time in a different manner than the 20 minutes each that we indicated, you are free to do so, but you need to tell us beforehand. In that case we would know that -- for example, that you are going to cross-examine the next witness for 60 minutes, one hour. But we would need to know it beforehand and the knowing beforehand means that you have got the consensus of all your -- your colleagues. In other words, we will not find ourselves in the situation then when Mr. Haynes will stand up and says but time is up, yes, but I need -- I need an hour, too. So this is what we tried to make clear when we handed down our decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: We understand that, Judge. I apologise. It's just that I guess we always usually speak to each other, so we know who is going to cross-examine and who is not; we're just not telling you up front. We will start doing that. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: One other suggestion. For Friday I have not mentioned this to the Defence, but since we know that it -- the submissions on the admissibility of intercepts is coming up, we would not object to having the Defence make oral submissions on this, and the Prosecution can as well, without prejudice or without the ability -- you know, not the -- so they can file afterwards as well. And this may save time in the long run, especially when the issue is we have admissibility versus weight and the law as you know in this Tribunal is rather clear on that. And so where they are going with suggesting these things are not admissable, I think it would be interesting to hear. And orally it shouldn't -- it shouldn't -- it shouldn't be a great burden on anyone by Friday to come up with some oral argument.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. McCloskey. And, of course, needless to say, that is an interesting suggestion. However, we gave the Defence teams up to the 2nd of February to file their position on -- on intercepts, and I think it will be pre-empting somewhat their -- the issue if we require them to stand up and -- and make oral submissions Friday, which is a few days before the dead-line. I don't know. I mean, I don't think that it would be appropriate. However, if the Defence teams are prepared to accept that, of course we can go along with your suggestion. Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. President, I tend to agree with you. However, one other suggestion would be, if Mr. McCloskey would like to stand up and then speak to the Trial Chamber and us and tell us why he thinks they are admissable, then I wouldn't have an objection with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Again, that would presume that he anticipates the nature of the objections that you will be filing on the 2nd of February. So asking him to answer in advance what he doesn't know is -- yeah. Anyway, let's leave it at that. 1.00 we resume the sitting. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everybody. And good afternoon to you, Witness. You are about to start giving evidence. Before you do so, you are required to enter a solemn declaration, as per the text that you are going to be handed now, that you will be testifying the truth in this trial. Please go ahead, read it out, and that will be your undertaking with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So please make yourself comfortable. Sir, we have put in place for you two protective measures, namely the use of a pseudonym instead of your name, and facial distortion. I trust these have been explained to you and that that arrangement is to your satisfaction. Could you confirm that, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. You are going to be first asked

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: made today. And he will then be followed by some of the Defence teams' cross-examination. However, you will probably need to return back tomorrow morning when we will finish with you. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon to Your Honour, counsel, everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, I'm handing to Madam Usher a sheet of paper and I am asking to you read it to yourself and confirm that your name is written next to PW-152. And for the record, the sheet is PO2396.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-152
utterances.text: Yes, that is my name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, we met to morning; is that correct? For the first time.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-152
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And you provided a witness statement; is that also correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-152
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Did you have in a statement read back to you in your own language?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-152
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Did you sign it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-152
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And can you attest, sir, to this Trial Chamber that the witness statement is true and accurate?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-152
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Can you further attest that your answers would be the same if you were asked the same questions reflected in that witness statement here in court?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-152
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, what I'd like to do now is to read a summary of your very brief witness statement. And then I just have one further question for you before the cross-examination will commence. Your Honour, if we may move into private session just for a moment, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sometime between December 1994 and early 1995 the witness was asked to serve in the Anti-Electronic Warfare Unit of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. He served at the southern site from early 1995 through October 1995. He described the shift lengths at the southern site, as well as the procedure he used when intercepting, taping, and transcribing radio communications. He reviewed photocopies of three handwritten intercepts and confirmed that he intercepted, recorded, and transcribed those three intercepts. He additionally reviewed three typewritten printouts and confirmed that those printouts contained the same conversation as the three he previously confirmed taking by hand. He noted that in his handwritten intercepts he wrote that Cerovic was a colonel or lieutenant-colonel and that in the printout he is identified as a colonel. He stated that this change may have been made by the typist alone or by him in consultation with his colleagues but he does not have a specific recollection. While there are one or two other minor differences between the handwritten and typed versions, none of those differences changes the meaning of the intercept. And for the record the full statement is PO2395. It's not in e-court, but -- but it should be. We have hard copies. The B/C/S translations should have been here by now. I apologise that they're not. They should be coming through the door any second, but the English translations have been furnished previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Just one question, sir. Did I show you three original intercept notebooks a few moments ago?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-152
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And were you able to identify the three handwritten intercepts contained in the packet that I showed you in those intercept notebooks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-152
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: In other words, you identified your handwritten intercepts in those three original notebooks; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-152
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I have no further questions at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Thayer. Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-152
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to remind you of your short statement to the Prosecution, so I would just like you to clarify a few things for me. You explained that you worked in shifts, and I would like to ask you to tell me, if you can, how many people worked in one shift. For example, the shift which you worked in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-152
utterances.text: In our unit there were between seven and 10 people, depending on the number who -- of people who came into the shift.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that the unit of seven to 10 men was divided into two shifts and then perhaps four or five people worked in one shift from seven to 10 days, like you said?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-152
utterances.text: During the day there were no set shifts. Everyone was there during the day. During the day we didn't have strict shifts; that didn't happen very often. The shifts were organised during the night.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you clarify, please, when you say seven to 10 people, do you consider that there were seven to 10 people at the facility at the same time, or you are thinking that there were seven to 10 people total in the unit who worked in these shifts?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-152
utterances.text: There were seven to 10 people at the facility during a shift at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Does that also apply to July 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-152
utterances.text: From what I can recall, I think that at the time there were between 10 and 11 people there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell me during the day how many people worked in one shift?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-152
utterances.text: Very often almost all the people who were at the facility were present. I'm talking about during the day. During the night we worked in shifts; three people would cover the night, and then during the day whenever anyone was free, they would be present at the facility together with the others who were working that -- on that job.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So can you please tell me how many workstations you had at the facility in this period of July 1995. We're interested in that period.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-152
utterances.text: From what I can remember, I think we had four to five devices or sets.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please tell me which devices they were? Do you remember, can you remember the -- the brand names?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-152
utterances.text: I really don't remember. I'm not a technician by profession, so I have no -- not much knowledge about the devices.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you have any idea about the antennas that were used?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-152
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You also said in your statement that on several occasions you typed in these intercepts that you noted down into the computer. Can you please explain -- first, can you confirm whether this is true or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-152
utterances.text: Yes, it is. It's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you remember if, when you were typing in the intercepts, you typed in the dates yourself into the computer or was this something that the computer generated automatically?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-152
utterances.text: I think that we did type in the date and the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember if you typed in the number under which the intercept was being sent?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-152
utterances.text: No, I -- I don't remember. I think the documents were sent with separate numbers. I said that in the statement. I did not send off the report in its final version. When the main operator was not there, then the intercept operators would type them out, but only the main operator or the commander would actually send them out. We would just type in our own reports that were brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that you did not assign a number to the report and that this was done by the person who sent the final version off?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-152
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zivanovic. Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I have no further questions and maybe I'm too late, because Mr. Zivanovic had some cross-examination. I polled the Defence counsel, I think everybody is giving their time to Natasha. Okay. Excuse me, Mr. Gregurevic has changed his mind. He has maybe 10 minutes. I believe everybody else is willing to give their time to Natasha.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly. Yeah, okay. We haven't received interpretation. Madam Fauveau is seeking leave to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Permission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- briefly in the hope of being able to finish the cross-examination today. Yes, by all means. You need the assistance of the security? I don't know how you are going to do that. But what I suggest is that General Miletic walks out with you, or approaches you. I don't know. If he's going to leave the courtroom, while Mr. Lazarevic proceeds with his cross-examination, then obviously we need his consent to proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it will only take two minutes, Mr. President, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think you can either approach -- I think Mr. -- General Miletic, I don't know how you're going to do this, but whichever way you think. Mr. Lazarevic, in the meantime, I think you can start with your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, it's going to be a very brief one.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-152
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: When we talk about the location where you worked we will not refer to it by its name, I will talk about it as the southern location to distinguish it from others so that you are clear on that point. May I ask you just a few preliminary questions. From what your statement we have just received and the summary the Prosecutor has given us, I don't find any information regarding your training for the job that you did in 1994 and 1995. Did you receive any kind of training for that job?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-152
utterances.text: When I arrived at the facility I was trained by the operators who worked there before. It was very simple, they just showed me the frequencies and the way to use the equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Before that you had no prior experience, no preparations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-152
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: To avoid overlapping, I know you understand me without any interpretation, but please wait until I have finished with my question before you begin answering. Before that training you received there and it was not very complicated, did your superiors - and please don't mention them for the sake of protecting your own identity - point out to you some of the speakers under surveillance to which you should pay particular attention?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-152
utterances.text: Yes. Some names were already well known on certain frequencies.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Was there by any chance any written record kept, any file that you kept on such persons where we could read General such and such, Colonel such and such occupying such and such a position in such and such unit, his characteristics of speech, frequently uses foul language, such and such accent, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-152
utterances.text: Not in our facility.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On that southern location where you were based -- I withdraw that. Do you know the term 28th Division?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-152
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And we will agree that it was a unit, a division from Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-152
utterances.text: That's what we heard officially.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: At that southern location where you were based, there was a communications unit; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-152
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Just one more question about this. Do you know that this communications unit was an intermediary in communications between the 28th Division and the superior command in Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-152
utterances.text: No, I had no such information. They were not in the same room with us, and we did not have such intensive contacts.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I have no further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you so much, Mr. Lazarevic. Before passing on the floor to Madam Fauveau, I just want to confirm that no other Defence team wishes to cross-examine this witness. Madam Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: [No audible answer]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I want to assure you, I don't need all that time, actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... use.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, you said that sometimes you typed your intercepts on the computer. I would like you to confirm that the people who intercepted in the site you were could themselves type directly on the computer the intercepts. Could you confirm this, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-152
utterances.text: Yes, with the leave of the commander who was present.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it true that the commander had direct access to the computer?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-152
utterances.text: In the event that the operator did not show up, I think the commander was authorised to use the computer.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I would like now the witness to be shown 1281B, the Exhibit 1281B. For the English version, it's 1281A. Maybe for the witness it would be preferable to be shown the original notebook. I want to ask you my question while you are being given the notebook. It's about the intercept at the bottom of the page starting at 9.49. One can see that you identified Captain Lucic, and for the moment I'll just stop there.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-152
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Could you look at this intercept and tell us how you managed to identify Captain Lucic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-152
utterances.text: I really couldn't answer that question now. And I don't want to speculate whether this Captain Lucic had been mentioned before.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: When you say that it might have been mentioned before, is it true that when you were transcribing this conversation you had to jot it down exactly as it was so you should have mentioned his name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-152
utterances.text: The conversation had to be transcribed the way it was recorded. There is a possibility that another conversation was already recorded on the tape that we had not had time to listen to. I cannot remember the details precisely, but I don't see any reason why.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it true therefore that sometimes you were taping a new intercept before having finished transcribing the previous, already-taped conversation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-152
utterances.text: It was not possible, because -- I mean, you could do that on another set of equipment, but you could not start recording something new on the same tape before listening to what was on the --

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Perhaps I didn't understand what you said. I will read out what you just said to my previous question. "[In English] There is a possibility that another conversation was already recorded on the tape that we had not had time to listen to." [Interpretation] Could you explain what you mean?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-152
utterances.text: No, I didn't say that it was recorded on the tape. Maybe there was in a prior part, a reference to Captain Lucic. Before the recording started there may have been a part of the conversation where Captain Lucic was mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: When such a situation arises, weren't you obliged to say that a part of the conversation had not been taped but that you heard a name or part of this intercept? Were you not supposed to report that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-152
utterances.text: No, we just wrote down the part that was recorded on tape.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Therefore, if somebody wanted to check whether it was indeed properly transcribed and corresponded exactly to the tape, it was indeed impossible because the transcription did not effectively correspond exactly to what was taped; isn't it the case?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-152
utterances.text: I don't understand. Why wouldn't it correspond?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Let's take this example. If somebody took the tape of this intercept, he wouldn't have heard the name of Captain Lucic anywhere; isn't it true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-152
utterances.text: One would need to play back the tape. Now I cannot tell you exactly whether there was a reference to him before that or not, because I recorded only this part of the conversation.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I would now like to call your attention on another point. Indeed you spoke about this in your statement. It's about Colonel or Lieutenant-Colonel Cerovic. Twice you indicate colonel or lieutenant-colonel. Does this mean you were not sure of what you heard?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-152
utterances.text: It was not very well audible on the tape, whether they said colonel or lieutenant-colonel.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... 1281C, Exhibit 1281C, please. Sir, on this report Colonel Cerovic features there. His name is indicated there. You already explained you didn't know if it was the person who typed the report or yourself who corrected this. But isn't it true that the report which was typed should have exactly corresponded to what had been jotted down by the interceptor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-152
utterances.text: When this report is sent, at that time the operator types in the part that he is hearing and I think in this part of the statement I can't remember exactly at the suggestion of my commander or somebody else, they told me that -- I was given to understand that he was a colonel, so in the final paper that I produced he was designated as a colonel.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Therefore I'm going to be try to be very clear. The fact that Colonel Cerovic is indicated on this document is indeed thanks to the fact that a member of your team knew, but it is not what you heard during the intercept. And when I say it is not what you heard, I don't mean that you didn't hear that, but you were not sure of having heard precisely this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-152
utterances.text: If you look at the original document you will see that it says "Colonel Cerovic" on the top. But there was the slightest degree of uncertainty and that's why it was written lieutenant-colonel below.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: That's precisely what I am telling you. You were not sure when you heard the intercept, you were not sure of what you heard, and somebody told you that the person in question was Colonel Cerovic, somebody who knew the rank of this person. Is it not so?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-152
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, could I confer one minute with my client, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have no other questions to ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Fauveau. Mr. Thayer, do you have any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We don't have any further questions for you, sir, which means that your testimony finishes here. Madam Usher will escort you out of the courtroom and the rest of our staff will -- one moment, I haven't finished. And the rest of the staff will assist you to facilitate your return home. On behalf of the Tribunal, I wish to thank you for having come over to give evidence, and I also wish you a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let's proceed with the tendering process. There are the usual two documents, one being the witness statement dated 24th of January, which will go under seal, as Exhibit PO2395, and then there is the pseudonym sheet will go under seal as PO2396.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are there objections in relation to the three intercepts that are being tendered? I hear none. So these three intercepts will be marked for identification. The understanding that the ones appearing in both characters in the sheet that has been distributed by the Prosecution will be kept under seal. I think we can safely say that that concludes the business for today. Do I take it that tomorrow morning we will see Ms. Frease again, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, that's the plan. I have asked Mr. Vanderpuye to tell me -- to work as hard as he could to do that. I have not heard back from him. I think he is probably working with Ms. Frease right now. And I will let everyone know if there is any problems, but otherwise that's what we're shooting for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you so much, Mr. McCloskey. So we will adjourn to tomorrow morning at 9.00. I wish you all a happy afternoon and evening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
